rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Which of the following ligands is an ambidentate ligand ?
rows.solution:
The THIOCYANATE ion, \(\mathrm{SCN^-}\), is the ambidentate ligand.

An AMBIDENTATE ligand has TWO DIFFERENT donor atoms but binds through only ONE of them at a time. The thiocyanate ion offers a sulphur and a nitrogen: bound through sulphur it is named thiocyanato-S, and through nitrogen thiocyanato-N, or isothiocyanato. The two give different compounds — an instance of LINKAGE isomerism.

The other three each have a single kind of donor atom and so no choice to make: carbon monoxide donates through its carbon, ammonia through its nitrogen, water through its oxygen.

Note that ambidentate is not the same as bidentate. A bidentate ligand uses two donor atoms AT ONCE, closing a chelate ring; an ambidentate one merely has two to choose between.

rows.stem: On adding \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution to 1 mole of \(\mathrm{CoCl_3 \cdot 4NH_3}\), one mole of AgCl is precipitated. The secondary valency of Co is :
rows.solution:
The secondary valency is SIX.

Silver nitrate precipitates only the chloride that is FREE IN SOLUTION. One mole of silver chloride from one mole of complex means just ONE chloride is outside the coordination sphere — so the other TWO must be inside, acting as ligands.

The formula is therefore \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]Cl}\).

Secondary valency is Werner's term for the COORDINATION NUMBER, the count of donor atoms bonded directly to the metal: four ammonia molecules plus two chlorido ligands gives SIX, and the geometry is octahedral.

The primary valency here is 3, corresponding to cobalt's \(+3\) oxidation state — check it: two chlorido ligands give \(-2\) and four ammonias are neutral, so the complex ion is \(+1\) and needs the one chloride outside.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following elements of 3d series of transition elements has the lowest \(\Delta_{\mathrm{a}}\mathrm{H^{o}}\) ?
rows.solution:
ZINC has the lowest enthalpy of atomisation.

Enthalpy of atomisation measures the energy needed to pull a metal's atoms apart into free gaseous atoms — in other words, to overcome the metallic bonding. In a transition metal that bonding is strong because the \((n-1)d\) electrons take part in it alongside the \(ns\) electrons.

Zinc is \(3d^{10}4s^2\): its d subshell is completely filled, so those electrons are all paired and contribute NOTHING to the bonding. Only the two \(4s\) electrons do, the interatomic forces are correspondingly weak, and \(\Delta_a H^{\circ}\) is only about 126 kJ per mole.

Chromium is at the other extreme with six unpaired electrons and about 397 kJ per mole. Scandium and copper fall in between.

The same fact shows up as zinc's low melting point, 693 K, and as its softness.

rows.stem:
Consider the following reaction :
\(\mathrm{4-HO-C_6H_4-CH_2-OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}} ?\)
The major product obtained is :
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the reactant AND all four options are printed only as DRAWN ring structures; the stem names nothing in words. Every ring here is aromatic (Kekule, inner double bonds - checked at magnification). On the page: the reactant is a ring bearing CH2OH with OH para to it; (A) a ring bearing CH2-Cl with Cl para; (B) a ring bearing CH2-Cl with OH para; (C) a ring bearing CH2OH with Cl para; (D) a TRISUBSTITUTED ring bearing CH2OH, a halogen on the adjacent position, and OH para to the CH2OH. Transcribed above as condensed formulas with locants, which is a lossless reading and does not state which OH the reagent attacks. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The major product is \(\mathrm{4{-}HO{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2{-}Cl}\), 4-(chloromethyl)phenol.

The molecule carries TWO hydroxyl groups — one ALCOHOLIC, on the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) side chain, and one PHENOLIC, on the ring. Thionyl chloride attacks only the alcoholic one.

The phenolic hydroxyl is unreactive towards it, because its \(\mathrm{C-OH}\) bond has partial double bond character from resonance with the ring — the oxygen's lone pair is fed into the ring, shortening and strengthening the bond — so it will not break to let chloride substitute.

So the chlorine replaces the side-chain hydroxyl and the ring hydroxyl is left alone. The option replacing both, and the one replacing only the ring hydroxyl, both ignore that difference; the last option substitutes on the ring itself, which thionyl chloride does not do.

rows.stem: Which of the following Grignard reagent will be used with methanal to prepare \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-CH_2-OH}\) ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the ring in the stem and the rings in options (A), (B) and (D) are drawn as PLAIN hexagons (no inner bonds), i.e. CYCLOHEXYL, while option (C) alone is drawn as a Kekule ring, i.e. PHENYL. Checked at 5x magnification; the official key (D) is consistent only with the cyclohexyl reading. That ring-type contrast is the whole discriminator and is carried above as C6H11 versus C6H5. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
The reagent is CYCLOHEXYLMAGNESIUM BROMIDE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}{-}MgBr}\).

Work backwards from the product. A Grignard reagent adds to a carbonyl carbon, and with METHANAL — the only aldehyde carrying two hydrogens there — the product after hydrolysis is a PRIMARY alcohol with ONE CARBON MORE than the reagent:
\(\mathrm{R{-}MgBr} + \mathrm{HCHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{R{-}CH_2OH}\)

The target is \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}{-}CH_2{-}OH}\), so \(\mathrm{R{-}CH_2OH}\) with \(\mathrm{R} = \mathrm{C_6H_{11}}-\), the cyclohexyl group.

The first two distractors already carry that extra \(-\mathrm{CH_2}-\) and would give an alcohol one or two carbons too long. And \(\mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr}\) is PHENYL, not cyclohexyl — an aromatic ring where a saturated one is wanted.

rows.stem: \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-CH_3}\) when treated with excess HI gives :
rows.solution:
With EXCESS hydrogen iodide, dimethyl ether gives TWO MOLECULES OF IODOMETHANE.

The first cleavage gives one molecule of the halide and one of the alcohol:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}O{-}CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3I} + \mathrm{CH_3OH}\)

But the methanol so formed is itself an alcohol, and with MORE hydrogen iodide available it too is converted:
\(\mathrm{CH_3OH} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3I} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Overall: \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}O{-}CH_3} + 2\mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{CH_3I} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The word EXCESS is doing all the work in this question. With only ONE equivalent of the acid the reaction stops at the first stage, and the answer would have been the halide and the alcohol. Note also that this second stage is only possible because the group is ALKYL — an aryl ether stops at the phenol, which hydrogen iodide cannot touch.

rows.stem: Which of the following compounds will not react with benzene sulphonyl chloride ?
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — option (D) alone is printed as a DRAWN Kekule benzene ring bearing NH2 (confirmed at 5x); options (A) to (C) are printed as text formulas. The drawing is aniline and is named losslessly above, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
TRIETHYLAMINE, \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_3N}\), does not react.

Benzenesulphonyl chloride — Hinsberg's reagent — attacks through a NITROGEN-HYDROGEN bond: the nitrogen's lone pair attacks the sulphur and a hydrogen is lost as the sulphonamide forms.

A TERTIARY amine has NO hydrogen on its nitrogen at all, so no sulphonamide can form and the amine is recovered unchanged. That is what makes the test a three-way one.

The other three all react. Ethylamine and aniline are PRIMARY and give sulphonamides that keep one acidic hydrogen on nitrogen, so their products dissolve in alkali. Diethylamine is SECONDARY and gives a sulphonamide with no hydrogen left, so its product is insoluble in alkali.

Soluble precipitate, insoluble precipitate, no reaction — one reagent separating all three classes.

rows.stem: 'Scurvy' is caused by the deficiency of vitamin :
rows.solution:
Scurvy is caused by a deficiency of VITAMIN C, ascorbic acid.

Vitamin C is needed to make collagen, the protein that holds connective tissue together, so without it the gums bleed, wounds fail to heal and the teeth loosen. It is WATER SOLUBLE, so the body cannot store a reserve and a regular supply is needed — which is why the disease appeared on long sea voyages and was cured by citrus fruit.

Of the others: vitamin E deficiency increases the fragility of red blood cells, vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, and vitamin D deficiency causes rickets.

rows.stem: The half life of a first order reaction with rate constant (k) of 3 \(\mathrm{min^{-1}}\) is :
rows.solution:
For a FIRST ORDER reaction the half-life is
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{k}\)

Substituting \(k = 3\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\):
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0{\cdot}693}{3} = 0{\cdot}231\ \mathrm{min}\)

The units confirm the step: dividing a pure number by a reciprocal time leaves a time, and it comes out in minutes because the constant was given in reciprocal minutes.

The trap is \(0{\cdot}693 \times 3 = 2{\cdot}31\), offered as a distractor — multiplying instead of dividing. A quick sanity check catches it: a LARGE rate constant means a FAST reaction, so the half-life must be SHORT, and 0.231 min is short while 2.31 min is not.

Note that this half-life contains no concentration term at all, which is the distinguishing feature of first order.

rows.stem: Which of the following cells is used in hearing aids ?
rows.solution:
The MERCURY CELL is used in hearing aids.

Its virtue is a CONSTANT POTENTIAL of about \(1{\cdot}35\) V throughout its life. The reason is structural: its overall reaction, zinc with mercury(II) oxide giving zinc oxide and mercury, involves no ion in solution whose concentration can change, so there is nothing in the Nernst quotient to shift.

A hearing aid, like a watch or a pacemaker, needs a supply that does not drift as it is used, and the mercury cell's small size suits it as well.

The dry cell is the contrast: its reaction produces and consumes ions in the paste, so its voltage falls steadily. The nickel-cadmium cell is a rechargeable secondary cell used where more power is wanted, and a fuel cell needs a continuous supply of fuel from outside.

rows.stem: Aniline on reaction with Bromine water gives :
rows.solution:
Aniline with bromine water gives 2,4,6-TRIBROMOANILINE, as a white precipitate.

All three available positions are substituted at once, and no catalyst is needed. The amino group is so strongly activating — its lone pair is fed into the ring, raising the electron density most at the ortho and para positions — that even the feeble electrophile present in bromine water suffices.

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3NH_2} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)

Stopping at a MONObromo product requires the amino group to be MODERATED first: acetylate it, brominate the acetanilide, then hydrolyse. That route gives p-bromoaniline, which is offered here as a distractor — the right product from the wrong conditions.

The meta isomer is never a significant product, because the amino group does not activate that position.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}\mathrm{H}\) and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}\mathrm{V}\) are zero for an ideal solution.
Reason (R) : The solution which obeys Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration is called an ideal solution.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

\(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H\) and \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V\) ARE zero for an ideal solution, and an ideal solution DOES obey Raoult's law over the entire range of concentration — both statements hold.

But the second does not EXPLAIN the first. Both are DEFINING properties of an ideal solution, listed side by side in its definition; neither causes the other. Saying that an ideal solution obeys Raoult's law is another way of identifying the same class of solution, not a reason why its enthalpy of mixing vanishes.

The actual explanation lies one level deeper: in an ideal solution the A-B interactions are the SAME in strength as the A-A and B-B interactions. Heat is absorbed or released only when the new interactions differ from those broken, so with all three alike the energy balances exactly and no heat flows — and, for the same reason, no volume change occurs and the escaping tendencies follow Raoult's law.

That underlying sameness explains both statements, which is why neither explains the other.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Rate of reaction decreases with increase in temperature.
Reason (R) : Number of effective collisions increases with increase in temperature.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is FALSE while the Reason is TRUE.

The rate of a reaction INCREASES with temperature, not decreases — near room temperature a rise of ten degrees roughly doubles or trebles it. The Assertion has the direction reversed.

The Reason is correct. What matters is the number of EFFECTIVE collisions — those carrying at least the activation energy and occurring in the right orientation — and the fraction of molecules with that much energy is \(e^{-E_a/RT}\), which climbs steeply as the temperature rises.

So the Reason states exactly why the Assertion is false: more effective collisions mean a FASTER reaction. Corrected, it would have explained the Assertion perfectly.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Phenol on reaction with aqueous NaOH gives sodium phenoxide.
Reason (R) : This reaction supports the acidic nature of phenol.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Phenol does react with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium phenoxide:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5O^-Na^+} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

And that reaction is exactly what demonstrates phenol's acidity. Only an ACID forms a SALT with a base — what leaves the phenol is the hydrogen of its hydroxyl group as \(\mathrm{H^+}\), and the phenoxide ion left behind is the conjugate base.

The comparison with an ALCOHOL makes the point sharper. Ethanol does NOT dissolve in sodium hydroxide, because it is far too weak an acid; phenol does. The difference is that the phenoxide ion's charge is delocalised into the benzene ring by resonance while an alkoxide's is stuck on one oxygen — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 10 against about 16.

Phenol is nevertheless weaker than carbonic acid, so it does NOT dissolve in sodium hydrogencarbonate — which is how a phenol is told apart from a carboxylic acid.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Boiling point of butan-1-ol is higher than that of butan-1-amine.
Reason (R) : Being more polar, butan-1-ol forms stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonds as compared to butan-1-amine.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Butan-1-ol boils higher than butan-1-amine — about 391 K against 351 K — although the two have nearly the same molar mass and the same carbon skeleton.

The Reason gives the cause exactly. Boiling point here tracks the strength of the intermolecular HYDROGEN BONDING, and that depends on how polar the bond donating the hydrogen is. OXYGEN is more electronegative than nitrogen, so the \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond is more polar than the \(\mathrm{N-H}\) bond, and the hydrogen bonds it forms are correspondingly stronger.

Stronger association means more energy needed to separate the molecules, so the alcohol boils higher.

Note that the amine has TWO hydrogens on its nitrogen against the alcohol's one on oxygen, so it is not the NUMBER of hydrogen bonds that decides here but their STRENGTH — which is precisely what the Reason says.

rows.stem:
Write the reactions of glucose with :
(a) HI
(b) \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\)
rows.solution:
(a) WITH HYDROGEN IODIDE and red phosphorus on prolonged heating, D-glucose is reduced all the way to N-HEXANE:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{HI}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3}\)

Every oxygen is stripped out, and the product is a STRAIGHT chain of six carbons. That result is one of the classic proofs of glucose's structure: it shows the six carbons are joined in an UNBRANCHED chain, since a branched skeleton would have given a branched hexane.

(b) WITH ACETIC ANHYDRIDE, glucose is acetylated to GLUCOSE PENTAACETATE:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)

Five acetyl groups go on, and each one requires a hydroxyl group to attach to — which is how the FIVE hydroxyl groups of glucose are counted.

Together the two reactions settle the skeleton and the functional groups: an unbranched six-carbon chain carrying five hydroxyls.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem:
Complete and balance the following chemical equations :
(a) \(\mathrm{3MnO_4^{2-} + 4H^{+} \longrightarrow}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 14H^{+} + 6Fe^{2+} \longrightarrow}\)
rows.solution:
(a) The manganate ion DISPROPORTIONATES in acid — the same element is oxidised and reduced at once. Some manganese goes from \(+6\) up to \(+7\) as permanganate, the rest down to \(+4\) as manganese dioxide, and the green solution turns purple:
\(3\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}} + 4\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Check the balance: manganese 3 both sides; oxygen 12 on the left against \(8 + 2 + 2 = 12\); hydrogen 4 both sides; charge \(-6 + 4 = -2\) on the left against \(-2\) on the right.

(b) Dichromate oxidises iron(II) to iron(III) in acid, chromium falling from \(+6\) to \(+3\):
\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 14\mathrm{H^+} + 6\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 6\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Six electrons change hands: two chromiums take three each, and six iron(II) ions give up one each. This reaction is the basis of the volumetric estimation of iron, potassium dichromate being a primary standard.

rows.stem:
(a) Which halogen compound in the following pair will react faster in \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reaction and why ?
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-Cl}\)   OR   \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CHCl-CH_3}\)
(b) Why does the presence of nitro groups at ortho- and para- positions in haloarenes increase their reactivity towards nucleophilic substitution reaction ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — the two compounds in (a) are printed ONLY as skeletal zig-zag structures and are named nowhere in the stem. Read at 4x magnification: the left structure is a four-carbon chain with Cl on a terminal carbon, the right is a four-carbon chain with Cl on the second carbon; they are transcribed above as the corresponding condensed formulas, which is a lossless reading. The marking scheme redraws the LEFT structure as its answer and calls it the primary halide, which corroborates the reading. The word 'OR' between them is part of the printed stem and is NOT an internal choice. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) 1-CHLOROBUTANE, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl}\), reacts faster.

An \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction requires the nucleophile to attack the carbon from the side directly OPPOSITE the leaving group, so the rate is governed by how ACCESSIBLE that carbon is.

1-Chlorobutane is a PRIMARY halide: the carbon carrying the chlorine has two hydrogens and only one alkyl group, so the approach from behind is nearly unobstructed. 2-Chlorobutane is SECONDARY, with two alkyl groups on that carbon, and they get in the way.

Steric hindrance, not electronics, is what decides here — the order runs primary, secondary, tertiary, with tertiary halides essentially unreactive by this route. Note that the \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) order runs exactly the opposite way, because the same bulk that blocks the nucleophile STABILISES the carbocation.

(b) Because a nitro group at the ORTHO or PARA position STABILISES THE INTERMEDIATE CARBANION.

Nucleophilic substitution on a haloarene goes through a negatively charged intermediate, formed when the nucleophile adds to the ring carbon holding the halogen. The more stable that intermediate, the lower the energy barrier and the faster the reaction.

A nitro group is strongly electron withdrawing, and from the ortho or para position it can accept that negative charge RIGHT ONTO ITS OWN OXYGEN by resonance. It also pulls electron density out of the ring generally, which makes the ring less repellent to the approaching nucleophile in the first place.

The POSITION is essential: a nitro group at the META position cannot accept the charge by resonance and has almost no effect. Adding more o- and p-nitro groups helps further — chlorobenzene needs 623 K and 300 atmospheres to be hydrolysed, while 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene yields to warm water alone.
